restsrv01.polito.it server Debian 12

SSH access

Accessing the P4 switches is a straightforward ssh login using the hostnames in the previous table.

Important: this is a private testbed within Politecnico di Torino. Ask for VPN access if you are from a different organization

Connect to VMs through SSH

VMs are not directly visible on the PoliTO network, but are reachable by using restsrv01.polito.it as a bastion proxy. You have two options to connect.

  1. Connect via ssh to restsrv01.polito.it, and from there connect via ssh to your VM:
ssh <your user>@restsrv01.polito.it
ssh <your user>@<vm hostname>
  1. Single-step ssh using restsrv01.polito.it as a jump proxy:
ssh -J <your user>@restsrv01.polito.it <your user>@<vm hostname>

For convenience, you may want to add the following lines to your .ssh/config file. Replace:

Host <vm name>
 User <your user>
 ProxyCommand ssh <you user user>@restsrv01.polito.it -W %h:%p

You can then connect by only typing on your client:

ssh <vm name>

item.title: Network configuration
item.description:
This page describes the network architecture and the addressing scheme currently in use.

All compute and network nodes are connected to two subnets:

  • Dataplane network: this is a 100 Gbps networks with QSFP DAC cables. This is dedicated to experiments, traffic generation, etc. within the testbed
  • Management network: this is the network used to access the nodes via ssh.

Topology

All servers in the topology are equipped with two NICs at 100 Gbps. One NIC is connected to the P4 switches and one NIC is connected to a fixed-functions Cisco switch. Therefore, servers can communicate with each other without going through the Tofino switches, if a user doesn’t want so.

Open the network interconnection scheme

All VMs will be assigned two virtual network interfaces (vNICs) directly attached to the dataplane network (bridged mode). These interfaces are intended for experiments with the Tofino devices from within the VM.

Internet connectivity to the VMs is provided through a third interface (NAT mode), and must be exclusively used for control operations e.g., install packages.

IP addressing

The management network has IP subnet 192.168.24.64/26.
The dataplane network has IP subnet 10.10.0.0/24 and VLAN identifier 100.

The IP addresses of the management network have their corresponding DNS records and are not relevant to know.

item.title: Available resources
item.description:
Machines in the cluster are classified into compute nodes and network nodes, as described in cluster overview. The resource sharing policy is different for the two.

Access to P4 switches

The Edgecore Wedge100BF-32X switches available in the cluster feature:

  • Intel Tofino P4 programmable dataplane ASIC
  • x86 control plane CPU

Users can login on the switch CPU via normal e.g., ssh, start their program control-plane and push P4 programs to the Tofino ASIC.

Intel Tofino programmable data-plane hardware lacks native support for multi-tenancy (see About multi-tenancy in Tofino switches).

We restrict ssh access to the Tofino switches on a time-slotted basis, managed via a reservation mechanism. No more than one tenant at a time will be granted access.

A tenant willing to deploy and test its P4 code on SUP4RNET Tofino switches, must first reserve its own slot through a dedicated dashboard.

Prerequisite: you setup PoliTO VPN to access the dashboard.
Access the Tofino reservation dashboard

Once a slot has been reserved, a tenant will be granted exclusive access to the control plane CPU. The tenant can then login via ssh using the account he/she obtained and perform operations on the switch.

Developing P4 code from VMs

Each tenant can request one or more virtual machine (VM) on the compute nodes. Tenants can login on their VMs at their convenience, on which they have full control and root privileges.

VM images

VMs are primarily intended to let tenants to prototype their P4 code on the Intel Tofino Emulator, i.e., even without access to the physical Tofino ASIC.

VM images comes pre-configured as follows:

  • control plane IP address for ssh login
  • dataplane vNIC, bridged to a 100 Gbps dataplane network
  • Intel P4 Software Development Environment (SDE) and Intel Tofino emulator

VMs should also be privileged to run non-performance critical experiments whenever possible.

For performance critical experiments, the cluster offers (upon request) dataplane vNIC configured with PCI passthrough (SR-IOV), or direct access to the nodes.

Testing P4 code without access to Tofino ASIC

While the reservation mechanism to access the Tofino ASIC might be tedious, there is a way to prototype your P4 code on a Tofino emulator before deploying to the actual hardware. The Intel P4 SDE comes with a register-level Tofino emulator, which reproduces most of the pipeline features via software. Only some Tofino features are not supported by the emulator.

For all code that do not require these special features, we highly advise to first test your project on the emulator and move to the actual hardware when you are relatively confident about the correctness of your code.

This is especially recommended for inexperienced users for at least two reasons:

  1. A detailed log is available in the emulator and not on the ASIC
  2. You don’t create contention with other tentants when not necessary

About sudo privileges

All tenants are granted elevated privileges in their VMs. Instead, as a default policy, sudo privileges are disabled for all tenants on the switch OS and on the server OS. Should any user demand elevated permissions, it must ask the cluster admins. Only if strictly necessary, sudo privileges may be granted for specific commands and revoked when not needed anymore. In general, alternative solutions must be preferred.

item.title: General guidelines
item.description:
This page describes the development environment and tools we configured. It also provides a Tofino primer with some general advices and learned-by-doing facts, in order to speed up the learning curve for new students. This is not a comprehensive tutorial and assumes basic knowledge of the P4 ecosystem.

Join ICRP!

Make sure to join the Intel Connectivity Research Program private community. It’s a cool place where you fill find answers to many of your doubts. It is actively used and you will usually receive an answer within 24 hours.

Intel Connectivity Research Program (Private Forum)

Intel P4 Software Development Environment (SDE)

We ship on all nodes the Intel P4 SDE, installed under /opt/p4-sde/bf-sde-<x.y.z>. We have tested and installed version 9.13.2.

The SDE contains the Tofino P4 compiler, the drivers to interact with the Tofino data plane ASIC, and the Barefoot Runtime (BFRT) libraries to implement the control plane APIs. It also contains many examples showcasing the Tofino features.

The following are some useful items under the SDE root directory:

  • pkgsrc/p4-examples: this folder contains examples of P4_16 code and its control plane code. Every example is packaged in its own folder, follow the instructions on the README in the single folders.

  • run_p4_tests.sh: utility to run one of the previous examples with one click.

  • run_switchd.sh: starts the switch daemon that interacts with the target data plane device.

  • run_tofino_model.sh: starts an instance of the Intel Tofino Model. It is the software emulator to be used as target instead of the physical ASIC. See Tofino model.

  • run_bfshell.sh: connects a shell to an existing switch daemon. The shell can be used to configure ports, dump the P4 tables, and others. See Interactive bfshell.

  • install/share/tofinopd/ this folder contains the build artifacts of your P4 programs, context.json, bf-rt.json and the .bin compiled binary of your .p4 source code. See Build and run.

Recommended devolpment workflow

Use VS Code

To quickly edit and test your code without the need of syncronizing your local changes to the remote cluster machines, we strongly encourage you to familiarize yourself with the Remote Development Feature of the Visual Studio Code.

It allows editing code as if you were on a local filesystem.

While configuring your ssh access to the nodes, it is also advised to install your ssh key(s) on the remote nodes and add them to your ssh agent so that VS code stops prompting the passphrase from you.

Edit your PYTHONPATH

The Intel SDE provides several libraries and utilities written in Python to write your control plane scripts and interact with the switch. If you have installed the VS Code Python extension, it is useful while writing the code if VS Code is able to find the Python libraries of the Intel SDE for code linting and autocompletion.

A quick way is to add them to your PYTHONPATH variable.

The following instructions will have effect on the PYTHONPATH only while developing from VS Code in your project folder.

Create a file .envin your project folders with the following content:

PYTHONPATH="/opt/p4-sde/bf-sde-9.13.2/install/lib/python3.8/site-packages:/opt/p4-sde/bf-sde-9.13.2/install/lib/python3.8/site-packages/tofino:/opt/p4-sde/bf-sde-9.13.2/install/lib/python3.8/site-packages/tofino/bfrt_grpc:/opt/p4-sde/bf-sde-9.13.2/install/lib/python3.8/site-packages/p4testutils/"

This will help the linter and autocomplete. Then, to let the VS Code integrated terminal also find the SDE libraries, add the following content to your .vscode/settings.json inside the project directory:

{
 "terminal.integrated.env.linux": {
 "PYTHONPATH":
 "/opt/p4-sde/bf-sde-9.13.2/install/lib/python3.8/site-packages:/opt/p4-sde/bf-sde-9.13.2/install/lib/python3.8/site-packages/tofino:/opt/p4-sde/bf-sde-9.13.2/install/lib/python3.8/site-packages/tofino/bfrt_grpc:${workspaceFolder}/controller"
 }
}

Reload VS Code for the changes to have effect. If you prefer not repeating these steps for all of your projects, you can configure the same options with global user settings.

item.title: Initial configuration WedgeBF-32X
item.description:
This pages shares experience in configuring a Edgecore WedgeBF-32X switch.

This page does not replace the official . Consult the official documentation for preliminary and more detailed information.

Configure the management plane

Before installing the OS, the only way to connect with the switch is via a CLI available on the serial port.

If you connect with a serial cable (ask your network administrator) you will first access the Board Management Controller CPU (BMC). Here you find a minimal Linux-based software (OpenBMC) to performs a variety of management functions, including

  • reset orchestration
  • power management
  • voltage monitoring / fan control, etc.

If asked for login credentials, use the default administration account root with password 0penBmc (first character is a zero).

Make BMC reachable over the network

It’s good practice to make the BMC reachable on your local network, by assigning it an IP address and setting network configuration. This way you can connect to the management Ethernet port of the switch and ssh into the OpenBMC directly, without the need of the serial cable.

Remember that the BMC is your last hope when the main CPU will become unreachable, before physical intervention.

Use netplan, ifconfig or your favorite method to assign an IP address to the port, or make a static DHCP reservation.

Working with ssh is also considerably faster than working with the serial port which has much limited baud rate.

The management network cannot be the 192.168.0.0/24 subnet. This is because there is an internal network between the BMC CPU and the main CPU on that subnet.

In the following example, we show the configuration of the eth0 interface on the BMC CPU. This is interface is internally switched (i.e., on the same broadcast domain) to the main CPU. item.title: Intel SDE install
item.description:
This pages documents how to install Intel P4 Studio and P4 development tools.

Intel P4 Studio can be installed on any machine running a supported OS. In a common situation, you want to install it on the switch OS to have the ability to communicate with the Tofino ASIC via platform-specific drivers, and push your programs to the dataplane.

In our cluster, we installed Intel P4 Studio on the control-plane OS running on the WedgeBF-32X switches and in the users VMs.

Preliminary steps

  • Download the Intel P4 Studio software from Intel Resource and Documentation Center (RDC).
  • Choose a directory and extract the tarball there, e.g., /opt/p4-sde
  • Set the following environmental variables according to your SDE directory:
export SDE=/opt/p4-sde/bf-sde-9.13.2/
export SDE_INSTALL=/opt/p4-sde/bf-sde-9.13.2/install

Install for ASIC

This is meaningful only on a physical switch.

When installing on the switches, you must enable the SDE to operational mode ASIC, and you must compile the Board Support Package (BSP) drivers provided by Edgecore.

Install dependencies

To be run only once for a fresh installation on a new OS.
Execute the following script: 
sudo -E $SDE/p4studio/install-p4studio-dependencies.sh

Apply profile

P4 Studio offers you interactive and profile install modes. If you don’t have specific requirements, you can proceed with the profile mode. It consists into applying a pre-defined installation profile, which contains the desired SDE configuration such as dependencies and modules to compile. We use the following profile:

global-options:
 asic: true
features:
 bf-diags: {}
 bf-platforms:
 bsp-path: /opt/p4-sde/bf-reference-bsp-9.13.1.tgz
 drivers:
 tdi: false
 p4-examples:
 - p4-16-programs
 - p4-14-programs
 switch:
 profile: x1_tofino
 sai: true
architectures:
- tofino

The previous profile is currently located under $SDE/p4studio/profiles/all-tofino-bsp.yaml in both rest-bfsw01 and rest-bfsw02.

Make sure the bsp-path points to an existing path. Otherwise, download the BSP tarball.

Then run:

cd $SDE
p4studio/p4studio profile apply p4studio/profiles/all-tofino-bsp.yaml
The installation takes about an hour, we recommend running the previous command from a tmux or screen terminal.

Load kernel modules (recommended)

When you run bf_switchd on the switch, ASIC mode will be automatically selected. With this mode, among other thingsbf_switchd tries to set a PCI port between the Tofino ASIC and the CPU. This port is seen as dev_port 192 from a P4 program on a 2-pipe Tofino.

To let programmers use the PCI CPU port, we must load a kernel module (one of bf_kdrv or bf_kpkt).

Run the following: sudo $SDE_INSTALL/bin/bf_kdrv_mod_load $SDE_INSTALL

Difference between bf_kdrv and bf_kpkt

The difference is that if you use bf_kdrv driver, it allows you to access PCIe CPU port (send/receive packets using packet DMA) at the user-process level, using the specialized bf_pkt APIs, whereas if you use bf_kpkt driver, then the CPU PCIe port is exposed as a regular Linux network interface, and you can send/receive packets using any standard Linux methods: you can simply open a raw socket (e.g., you can use libpcap, you can use Scapy, Wireshark, etc).

Install for general-purpose server

If you not install it for ASIC, the procedure is the same, but you don’t have to compile the BSP driver, and you don’t have to load the kernel modules. You can pick one of the profiles under $SDE/p4studio/profiles/ and proceed with apply as above. Alternatively, use the interactive install mode, where you will be prompted for a list of questions:

cd $SDE
p4studio/p4studio interactive

item.title: Request account
item.description:
Steps to access the cluster

Sign NDA with Intel

You can skip this step if you do not plan to work with P4 switches

Access to Intel documentations and Intel software for Tofino programmable switch family is released under confidentiality and non disclosure agreement (NDA).

Hence, the very first step in order to work with the switches is to sign a personal NDA with Intel. The procedure is as follows:

  • The head of your research group must apply for joining the Intel® Connectivity Research Program.
  • Once the application is accepted, your research group will be assigned a new identifier rgrp_id.
  • From now on, all members of the research group can submit an application for themselves to join the program. Access Intel® Connectivity Research Program User Application and fill the form using for the Group ID field rgrp_id.
  • The head of your research group must then confirm your application.
  • Finally, you will receive an email from Intel (~1-5 days) granting access to the Intel Connectivity web portal and online resources. Follow the instructions in the email you will receive.

Obtain your credentials

It is at this point that you will be granted access to the testbed and to the internal documentation.

Credentials for your user will be created at this step. Contact our account manager and ask for a new user. You will be provided with your credentials for the following:

  • System login: to access cluster’s nodes, see Login instructions
  • Internal documentation describing the network topology, the addressing scheme, some basic experiments for connectivity check and a walkthrough primer to move the first steps. See Documentation

Set up VPN

This is not mandatory for Politecnico di Torino members

The cluster is hosted at Politecnico di Torino (PoliTO) and only reachable from PoliTO campus network. If you are outside of Politecnico di Torino, you will need a VPN connection from your site to PoliTO network.

In order to simplify the management of VPN accounts, the preferred choice is to establish a site-to-site VPN between your respective institution and Politecnico di Torino. This is a one-time installation overhead and will not be repeated when new members of the same research group will join.

  • You or the IT department of your institution must get in touch with the cluster admins e.g., via email.
  • You will be provided with a spreadsheet and receive further instructions to fill it.

Requests for individual VPN accounts are granted to Politecnico di Torino members and may be granted to external partners in the presence of special circumstances. This will be decided on a per-request basis.

item.title: Run P4 code on Tofino
item.description:
This page describes the very first steps to get your P4 code running on the Tofino ASIC.

These guidelines are rather general and apply to any P4 program you may want to run on the Tofino ASIC.

Overview

You should be aware of two components in the Tofino hardware:

  1. the Tofino data plane ASIC
  2. a local “control plane” CPU, locally connected to the ASIC via PCIe.

These two are physically packaged in the same pizza box chassis by the manufacturer (e.g., our Wedge100BF-32X Edgecore switches).

To run your code on the Tofino, you need to:

  1. compile the code
  2. push it to the Tofino ASIC.

Compilation can be done on any Linux machine with P4 Intel Studio installed. Once compiled, the P4 code must be pushed to the Tofino ASIC. This can be done either manually or via Barefoot Runtime gRPC APIs (not discussed here).

Recommended workflow

Make sure your code compiles!

We provide a pre-installed P4 Intel Studio in the default VMs. Here you can develop and compile your P4 code.

Make sure your code compiles correctly before moving to Tofino. Do not request access to the Tofino ASIC if your code does not compile.

Other than compiling, we strongly recommend also to test your code on the VM. The Intel P4 SDE comes with a register-level Tofino emulator, which reproduces most of the pipeline features via software. Only some Tofino features are not supported by the emulator.

See Testing P4 code without access to Tofino ASIC for more details on how to test within the VM.

Move to switch

Once compiled, the binaries must be installed (pushed) on the target Tofino ASIC to run on the switch.

It is at this point that makes sense you try to move to the physical switch.

Read how here: Tofino access.

To speed up prototyping, at this time we recommend cloning your source code on the local switch CPU (it is an ubuntu system!) and working directly on the switch.

Using a separate machine as build host requires a little extra effort to push the pipeline configuration on the target ASIC via Barefoot Runtime gRPC APIs, not needed if you work build and run locally.

Check the switch status

As other users may have being working on the switch before you, double check that the switch ASIC is not running any other P4 program. You can do so by killing the switchd process:

$ ps aux | grep bf_switchd
root 2017246 78.3 29.5 3882848 2372004 ? Sl Apr23 18164:53 bf_switchd --install-dir /opt/p4-sde/bf-sde-9.13.2/install --conf-file /opt/p4-sde/bf-sde-9.13.2/install/share/p4/targets/tofino/tf_honeypot.conf --init-mode=cold --status-port 7777

Then kill the processes:

$ sudo kill -9 2017246

You can merge the two commands in a single one:

$ sudo kill -9 $(ps aux | grep bf_switchd | awk '{print $2}')

or try to use pkill:

$ sudo pkill -9 bf_switchd

Build and run locally

This section assumes you chose the CPU aboard the switch as build host.

Login into the switch CPU, and enter your project directory.

Compile the P4 code

Assuming you have a program named program.p4 in your current directory, the fastest method to compile it is:

sudo p4-build program.p4
p4-build is a simple wrapper we wrote to simplify the compile command. It invokes a more involved CMake command under the hood to generate build artifacts, as explained in “P4 Studio SDE Install Guide - Appendix C". You can use the CMake command directly if you wish.

Push to ASIC

At this point you are ready to push the data plane to the Tofino target. To do so, just manually start the Intel switch daemon specifying the P4 program to push.

sudo $SDE/run_switchd.sh -p program

NOTE: you must not add the .p4 extension here. The SDE automatically will retrieve from the build directory the compiled P4 binary with .bin extension, a bf-rt.json describing the tables reachable from the control plane, etc. and configure the pipeline(s). If you prefer, we created a quick alias:

sudo p4 -p program
run_switchd or p4 run several commands with sudo, so it is recommended to run them with sudo in case any failure.

It will detect the Tofino ASIC, configure the pipeline with your program, and start an interactive Barefoot shell bfshell instance.

item.title: Managing reservations
item.description:
Edit Tofino reservations

To edit user’s reservations on Tofino switches, you can use the reservation dashboard.

As an administrator, you can:

  • View all reservations
  • Delete a reservation
  • Flag priority of a reservation

Admin login

Login with your credentials

Edit with dashboard

item.title: Managing Tenants
item.description:
This guide covers how to add and remove tenants from the P4 cluster. A tenant is a user (or group of users) with one or more dedicated virtual machines connected to the cluster network.

Before You Start

You need:

  • SSH access to restsrv01.polito.it with sudo permissions
  • Ansible installed on your local machine (v2.13.7 or later)
  • The p4-restart-polito repository cloned locally:
git clone https://github.com/sup4rnet/p4-restart-polito
cd p4-restart-polito
All commands below must be run from inside the p4-restart-polito directory.

Adding a New Tenant

There are two ways to add a tenant: the automated way (recommended) and the manual way (if you need more control or the tool fails).

Option A: Automated Workflow (Recommended)

The p4tenant CLI tool handles everything for you: it picks available IP addresses, edits all the config files, and runs Ansible.

1. Install the tool (one-time setup)

brew install uv # macOS
# or: pip install uv

That’s it. No other installation needed.

2. Add the tenant

Run the interactive wizard:

./p4tenant-cli add user

The tool will:

  1. Ask for your admin username (for SSH access)
  2. Ask for the new tenant’s username
  3. Ask how many VMs to create (default: 1)
  4. Automatically allocate IP addresses
  5. Show you exactly what files will be changed
  6. Ask for confirmation before making changes
  7. Optionally run Ansible to provision the VM

Example session:

$ ./p4tenant-cli add user

Select admin user:
 1. pgiaccone has inventory
 2. zhihaow has inventory
 3. Other (enter manually)

Choice: 1
ℹ Operating as admin: pgiaccone

Enter tenant username: jdoe
Enter email (optional): john.doe@polito.it
How many VMs to create? [1]: 1

Validating...
✓ Username 'jdoe' is available
✓ Allocated IPs: 10.10.0.21/24, 10.10.0.22/24

╭────────────────────────── Changes to apply ──────────────────────────╮
│ 1. group_vars/all.yaml Add 'jdoe' to restart_users │
│ 2. host_vars/restsrv01.yaml Add 'restvm-jdoe-01' to vms list │
│ 3. host_vars/restvm-jdoe-01.yaml [NEW] Create with dataplane_ipv4 │
│ 4. inventory.yaml Add 'restvm-jdoe-01' to vms.hosts │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

Apply changes? [y/n]: y
✓ All changes applied successfully

Run ansible-playbook? [y/n]: y
Running: ansible-playbook playbooks/adduser.yaml ...
✓ ansible-playbook completed successfully
Type ? at any prompt to see help. The tool validates everything and won’t let you make mistakes like using a duplicate username or an already-used IP address.

Non-interactive mode

If you already know all the parameters:

./p4tenant-cli add user -u jdoe -A pgiaccone -a -y

Options:

  • -u jdoe: tenant username
  • -A pgiaccone: your admin username
  • -a: run Ansible automatically after adding
  • -y: skip confirmation prompts

Adding a VM to an existing tenant

If a tenant needs an additional VM:

./p4tenant-cli add vm

The tool shows you the tenant’s existing VMs and suggests a name for the new one (e.g., restvm-jdoe-02).

Option B: Manual Workflow

Use this if the automated tool doesn’t work or you need fine-grained control.

Add username to global user list

Edit group_vars/all.yaml and add the username to restart_users:

restart_users:
 - zhihaow
 - pgiaccone
 - jdoe  # <-- add here

Add VM to server’s VM list

Edit host_vars/restsrv01.yaml and add the VM name:

vms:
 - restsrv01-smartdata01
 - restvm-dauin-01
 - restvm-jdoe-01  # <-- add here

Create host variables file

Create a new file host_vars/restvm-jdoe-01.yaml:

# Pick UNUSED IPs from 10.10.0.11-100 range
# Run "./p4tenant-cli ip-status" to see what's available
dataplane_ipv4:
 - 10.10.0.21/24
 - 10.10.0.22/24

# Users on this VM (MUST be a list, even for one user)
host_users:
 - jdoe

Common mistakes:

  • Forgetting the /24 after the IP address
  • Writing host_users: jdoe instead of a list with - jdoe
  • Using an IP that’s already taken (check with ./p4tenant-cli ip-status)

Add VM to Ansible inventory

Edit inventory.yaml and add under the vms group:

vms:
 hosts:
 # ... existing VMs ...
 restvm-jdoe-01:
 ansible_host: restvm-jdoe-01
 ansible_user: p4-restart
 vars:
 ansible_ssh_common_args: '-o ProxyCommand="ssh YOUR_USERNAME@restsrv01.polito.it -W %h:%p"'

Replace YOUR_USERNAME with your actual username on restsrv01.

Run the playbook

ansible-playbook playbooks/adduser.yaml -i inventory.yaml -K

The -K flag prompts for the sudo password (required on first run only).

Verify it worked

SSH into the new VM:

ssh -J YOUR_USERNAME@restsrv01.polito.it jdoe@restvm-jdoe-01

If you get host key warnings, add these flags:

ssh -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no -o UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null \
 -J YOUR_USERNAME@restsrv01.polito.it jdoe@restvm-jdoe-01

Removing a Tenant

When a tenant leaves the cluster, you need to delete their VMs and remove their user accounts from the switches and server.

Option A: Automated Workflow (Recommended)

./p4tenant-cli remove

The tool will:

  1. Show you a list of tenants to choose from
  2. Show the tenant’s VMs with checkboxes to select which to delete
  3. Show exactly what will be deleted and ask for confirmation
  4. Run Ansible to delete VMs and remove user accounts
  5. Update all configuration files

Example session:

$ ./p4tenant-cli remove

Select tenant to remove:
 1. jdoe (1 VM)
 2. mamanj (1 VM)

Choice: 1

VMs to delete:
 [x] restvm-jdoe-01

This will:
 - Delete 1 VM(s) from restsrv01
 - Remove user 'jdoe' from P4 switches
 - Remove user 'jdoe' from reservation system
 - Update configuration files

Confirm deletion? [y/n]: y
...
✓ Tenant 'jdoe' removed successfully

Non-interactive mode

./p4tenant-cli remove jdoe -A pgiaccone -y

Partial operations

# Only update config files (don't delete VMs)
./p4tenant-cli remove jdoe --skip-ansible

# Only run Ansible (don't update config files)
./p4tenant-cli remove jdoe --skip-config

Option B: Manual Workflow

Run the removal playbook

The removeuser.yaml playbook handles most of the work:

ansible-playbook playbooks/removeuser.yaml -i inventory.yaml

It will prompt for:

  • The username to delete
  • Confirmation (type DELETE to confirm)

The playbook automatically:

  • Shuts down and deletes all VMs containing that username
  • Removes the user from P4 switches
  • Removes the user from the reservation webapp
  • Removes the user from the physical server

You can skip prompts by passing variables:

ansible-playbook playbooks/removeuser.yaml -i inventory.yaml \
 -e user_to_delete=jdoe \
 -e confirm_deletion=DELETE

Update configuration files

After the playbook completes, manually remove the tenant from these files:

File What to remove
group_vars/all.yaml Remove username from restart_users list
host_vars/restsrv01.yaml Remove VM name from vms list
host_vars/restvm-jdoe-01.yaml Delete this entire file
inventory.yaml Remove VM entry from vms.hosts section

Quick Reference

p4tenant commands

Command Description
./p4tenant-cli add user Add a new tenant with VM(s)
./p4tenant-cli add vm Add a VM to an existing tenant
./p4tenant-cli remove Remove a tenant and their VMs
./p4tenant-cli list Show all tenants and their status
./p4tenant-cli ip-status Show IP allocation (used/available)
./p4tenant-cli apply <user> Re-run Ansible for an existing tenant

Ansible playbooks

Playbook Purpose
adduser.yaml Full onboarding (creates VM, configures switches, bootstraps VM)
removeuser.yaml Full offboarding (deletes VMs, removes user everywhere)
bootstrap-tofino.yaml Only configure P4 switches
bootstrap-vms.yaml Only configure VMs

Running specific stages

The adduser.yaml playbook supports tags:

# Only create VMs
ansible-playbook playbooks/adduser.yaml -i inventory.yaml --tags kvmconf

# Only configure P4 switches
ansible-playbook playbooks/adduser.yaml -i inventory.yaml --tags p4conf -K

# Only bootstrap VMs
ansible-playbook playbooks/adduser.yaml -i inventory.yaml --tags vmboot -K

Troubleshooting

“Permission denied” when running Ansible

Make sure you have:

  1. SSH access to restsrv01.polito.it
  2. Your SSH public key at ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub
  3. Sudo permissions on the target machines

VM creation fails

Check that:

  • The VM name doesn’t already exist in virsh list --all
  • There’s enough disk space on restsrv01
  • The IP addresses aren’t already in use

Can’t SSH into the new VM

  1. Wait a minute after creation for the VM to boot
  2. Make sure you’re using the proxy jump: -J user@restsrv01.polito.it
  3. Try with host key checking disabled (see SSH command above)

p4tenant tool errors

The tool creates backups in .p4tenant-backups/ before making changes. If something goes wrong:

# See what files were backed up
ls -la .p4tenant-backups/

# Restore a file if needed
cp .p4tenant-backups/inventory.yaml.bak inventory.yaml

item.title: Configure ports
item.description:
Before generating any traffic, you need to explicitly configure the ports you want to use. This page describes how to configure ports on the Tofino ASIC.

Overview

  • Preliminaries: port types
  • Configuring ports manually
  • Automating port configuration via scripts

Port types

In rough terms, you have two types of ports:

  • Front panel ports: these are the ports on the front panel of the switch (32 ports on our switches).
  • Internal ports: these are “special” internal ports on the switch that are not on the front panel. Some important examples of this are:
    • Ethernet ports connecting ASIC with the CPU
    • Recirculation ports

The Ethernet ports CPU <-> ASIC are very useful to send packets from the CPU to the Tofino ASIC and vice versa for simple experiments.

For detail about port management, please refer to Section 5 of Wedge 100B User Guide documentations (NDA required).

Wedge 100B User Guide

Use bfshell to configure ports

A first manual but simple way is to use the bfshell command line interface to configure ports.

In this case, configuration is done in the port manager (PM) of the Tofino switch:

  1. decide which port you need - Show
  2. adding port - Add
  3. enabling ports - Enable

After running a P4 program on Tofino, a bfshell instance will be opened for you. If not, just execute bfshell on your Tofino session. You need first to enter the port manager (ucli.pm) CLI:

bfshell> ucli
bf-sde> pm

Show ports

The show -a command shows the information of all available ports:

bf-sde.pm> show -a
-----+----+---+----+-------+----+--+--+---+---+---+--------+----------------+----------------+-
PORT |MAC |D_P|P/PT|SPEED |FEC |AN|KR|RDY|ADM|OPR|LPBK |FRAMES RX |FRAMES TX |E
-----+----+---+----+-------+----+--+--+---+---+---+--------+----------------+----------------+-
1/0 |23/0|132|3/ 4|10G |NONE|Au|Au|YES|DIS|DWN| NONE | 0| 0|
1/1 |23/1|133|3/ 5|10G |NONE|Au|Au|YES|DIS|DWN| NONE | 0| 0|
1/2 |23/2|134|3/ 6|10G |NONE|Au|Au|YES|DIS|DWN| NONE | 0| 0|
1/3 |23/3|135|3/ 7|10G |NONE|Au|Au|YES|DIS|DWN| NONE | 0| 0|
...

There are several columns in the output:

  • MAC: Tofino’s QUAD-MAC/block ID of this connection
  • D_P: Toino’s device port ID of this connection. The ID used in P4 programs, Python scripts, PTF and Diag commands of Tofino.
  • P/PT: Tofino’s pipe ID and pipe_local_port_id (this is the port number you will be using in your P4 program).
  • FEC: forwarding error correction setting, which must be one of NONE, FC, or RS. NONE disables forwarding error correction, FC refers to BASE-R FEC (Fire Code FEC) and RS refers to Reed-Solomon FEC (RS-FEC).
  • AN: Autonegotiation
  • ADM: ENB for enabled port and DIS for disabled port
  • OPR: DWN for down port and UP for up port
  • FRAMES RX and FRAMES TX: port counters
  • E: whether there is error frames
  • For the rest columns, please refer to Wedge 100B User Guide.

Port details

To show details on a single port:

show -a -p <conn_id/chnl> [-d] [-t]

where

  • -p <conn_id/chnl> is to show the information of a specific port (conn_id) and lane (chnl). Without -p, information of all available ports is shown.
  • -d to show the detailed output.
  • -a to show all ports including physical ports that have not been configured or enabled.

conn_id/chnl: QSFP connector number / QSFP lane number of this connection, where the QSFP connector number is the number shown on the Wedge 100B front panel, and the lane number shows the lane for a channelized connection, or 0 for a non-channelized connection such as a port configured for 100G.

Adding a Port

port-add <conn_id/chnl> <speed> <fec>

where

  • conn_id/chnl: QSFP connector number / QSFP lane number of this connection
  • speed: port nominal speed, which must be one of 1G, 10G, 25G, 40G, 50G, or 100G. Please see Section 5.5.1 QSFP lane restrictions on port creation of Wedge 100B User Guide for detailed speed restrictions
  • fec: forwarding error correction setting, which must be one of NONE, FC, or RS.
Refer to the Port parameters section for the parameters to use when adding ports.

For example, adding a 100G port on dataplane port D_T=132, can be done as follows:

bf-sde.pm> port-add 1/- 100G NONE
bf-sde.pm> show
-----+----+---+----+-------+----+--+--+---+---+---+--------+----------------+----------------+-
PORT |MAC |D_P|P/PT|SPEED |FEC |AN|KR|RDY|ADM|OPR|LPBK |FRAMES RX |FRAMES TX |E
-----+----+---+----+-------+----+--+--+---+---+---+--------+----------------+----------------+-
1/0 |23/0|132|3/ 4|100G |NONE|Au|Au|YES|DIS|DWN| NONE | 0| 0|
1/1 |23/1|133|3/ 5|100G |NONE|Au|Au|YES|DIS|DWN| NONE | 0| 0|
1/2 |23/2|134|3/ 6|100G |NONE|Au|Au|YES|DIS|DWN| NONE | 0| 0|
1/3 |23/3|135|3/ 7|100G |NONE|Au|Au|YES|DIS|DWN| NONE | 0| 0|

where 1/- is a wildcard operation, which automatically fills with lane number.

Lane number. Every 100G port is split into 4 lanes. This allows to physically connect 4 25G transceivers to a single 100G port (port breakthrough). We do not support port breakout, therefore you can use the wildcard operation and forget about the lane number.

Enabling a Port

Finally, after adding a port, it is administratvely disabled by default. You need to enable it before using it.

port-enb <port_str>

where <port_str> is as same as <conn_id/chnl>.

For example:

bf-sde.pm> show -p 1/0
-----+----+---+----+-------+----+--+--+---+---+---+--------+----------------+----------------+-
PORT |MAC |D_P|P/PT|SPEED |FEC |AN|KR|RDY|ADM|OPR|LPBK |FRAMES RX |FRAMES TX |E
-----+----+---+----+-------+----+--+--+---+---+---+--------+----------------+----------------+-
1/0 |23/0|132|3/ 4|10G |NONE|Au|Au|YES|DIS|DWN| NONE | 0| 0|


bf-sde.pm> port-enb 1/0

Then note ADM column:

bf-sde.pm> show -p 1/0
-----+----+---+----+-------+----+--+--+---+---+---+--------+----------------+----------------+-
PORT |MAC |D_P|P/PT|SPEED |FEC |AN|KR|RDY|ADM|OPR|LPBK |FRAMES RX |FRAMES TX |E
-----+----+---+----+-------+----+--+--+---+---+---+--------+----------------+----------------+-
1/0 |23/0|132|3/ 4|10G |NONE|Au|Au|YES|ENB|DWN| NONE | 0| 0|

Disabling a Port

port-dis <port_str>

For example,

bf-sde.pm> show -p 1/0
-----+----+---+----+-------+----+--+--+---+---+---+--------+----------------+----------------+-
PORT |MAC |D_P|P/PT|SPEED |FEC |AN|KR|RDY|ADM|OPR|LPBK |FRAMES RX |FRAMES TX |E
-----+----+---+----+-------+----+--+--+---+---+---+--------+----------------+----------------+-
1/0 |23/0|132|3/ 4|10G |NONE|Au|Au|YES|ENB|DWN| NONE | 0| 0|
bf-sde.pm> port-dis 1/0
bf-sde.pm> show -p 1/0
-----+----+---+----+-------+----+--+--+---+---+---+--------+----------------+----------------+-
PORT |MAC |D_P|P/PT|SPEED |FEC |AN|KR|RDY|ADM|OPR|LPBK |FRAMES RX |FRAMES TX |E
-----+----+---+----+-------+----+--+--+---+---+---+--------+----------------+----------------+-
1/0 |23/0|132|3/ 4|10G |NONE|Au|Au|YES|DIS|DWN| NONE | 0| 0|

Deleting a Port

port-del <port_str>

For example:

bf-sde.pm> show -p 1/0
-----+----+---+----+-------+----+--+--+---+---+---+--------+----------------+----------------+-
PORT |MAC |D_P|P/PT|SPEED |FEC |AN|KR|RDY|ADM|OPR|LPBK |FRAMES RX |FRAMES TX |E
-----+----+---+----+-------+----+--+--+---+---+---+--------+----------------+----------------+-
1/0 |23/0|132|3/ 4|10G |NONE|Au|Au|YES|DIS|DWN| NONE | 0| 0|
bf-sde.pm> port-del 1/0
bf-sde.pm> show -p 1/0
-----+----+---+----+-------+----+--+--+---+---+---+--------+----------------+----------------+-
PORT |MAC |D_P|P/PT|SPEED |FEC |AN|KR|RDY|ADM|OPR|LPBK |FRAMES RX |FRAMES TX |E
-----+----+---+----+-------+----+--+--+---+---+---+--------+----------------+----------------+-
bf-sde.pm> show
-----+----+---+----+-------+----+--+--+---+---+---+--------+----------------+----------------+-
PORT |MAC |D_P|P/PT|SPEED |FEC |AN|KR|RDY|ADM|OPR|LPBK |FRAMES RX |FRAMES TX |E
-----+----+---+----+-------+----+--+--+---+---+---+--------+----------------+----------------+-
1/1 |23/1|133|3/ 5|10G |NONE|Au|Au|YES|DIS|DWN| NONE | 0| 0|
1/2 |23/2|134|3/ 6|10G |NONE|Au|Au|YES|DIS|DWN| NONE | 0| 0|
1/3 |23/3|135|3/ 7|10G |NONE|Au|Au|YES|DIS|DWN| NONE | 0| 0|

Port parameters

These parameters have been tested. Other choices may work, but not tested.

When adding ports, please use the following parameters:

Port Type DEV_PORT Speed FEC
Internal CPU Port 64-67 10G None (BF_FEC_TYP_NONE)
Front Panel Ports others 100G RS (BF_FEC_TYP_RS)

Recirculation ports 68-71 are automatically added by the bfswitchd upon instantiations and do not need to be configured explicitly.

🚀 Scriping port configuration

Manual port configuration is okay for a few ports, but if you need to configure many ports, it is better to use a script.

Simple Python script

You can create a Python script config_ports.py that looks like:

pm = bfrt.port

# enable internal CPU ports
pm.port.add(DEV_PORT=64, SPEED="BF_SPEED_10G", FEC="BF_FEC_TYP_NONE", PORT_ENABLE=True)
pm.port.add(DEV_PORT=66, SPEED="BF_SPEED_10G", FEC="BF_FEC_TYP_NONE", PORT_ENABLE=True)

# front panel port 2/0 directly attached to server
pm.port.add(DEV_PORT=140, SPEED="BF_SPEED_100G", FEC="BF_FEC_TYP_RS", PORT_ENABLE=True)

# front panel port 31/0 directly connected to 32/0
pm.port.add(DEV_PORT=128, SPEED="BF_SPEED_100G", FEC="BF_FEC_TYP_RS", PORT_ENABLE=True)
pm.port.add(DEV_PORT=136, SPEED="BF_SPEED_100G", FEC="BF_FEC_TYP_RS", PORT_ENABLE=True)

bfrt.complete_operations()

Then execute this script in the bfshell CLI:

$ bfshell -b config_ports.py

BFRuntime Python API

An even more advanced alternative is to use the Barefoot Runtime (BFRuntime) Python API to configure ports. This is a more advanced option not discussed here.

The BFRuntime API allows you to programmatically configure ports and other aspects of the Tofino switch from your Python control plane application.

Please check under /opt/p4-sde/bf-sde-9.13.2/ for examples.

item.title: Ping test
item.description:
Test connectivity with Intel switch.p4

The switch.p4 program is the L2/L3 P4 switch provided by Intel. It implements standard switching and routing functionalities you would find in a fixed-function switch, including features such as ACL, load balancing, etc.

We will use this P4 program for basic connectivity tests.

For other .p4 programs you are responsible to program the switch forwarding logic yourself. The following tests will not work as-it-is.

Intel provides a dedicated switch.p4 CLI that implements CRUD (Create, Read, Update, Delete) operations to interact with switch.p4. For these examples, we adopt the switch.p4 CLI to configure the switch program.

All the hosts involved in these experiments are on the same LAN, i.e., we will use only L2 features of switch.p4. At the very minimum, we must enable switch ports and add them to the default switch VLAN (with vlan_id 1), exactly as we would do in a fixed-function switch.

The following experiments assume the cable layout described in Network configuration.

server ↔️ switch.p4 ↔️ rest-bfsw01 cpu

In this scenario we test connectivity between a server, e.g., restsrv01, and a local control plane CPU on board of the P4 switches, e.g., rest-bfsw01. We directly connect the server to the P4 switch with no other hop in between.

First enable the switch ports.

The switch.p4 API expects a list of “lane identifiers” when we have to enable a port. Lane number can be obtained from the front panel port number with the following conversion: lane_number = (front_port - 1) x 4 
# enable port connecting rest-bfsw01 to restsrv01
add port type NORMAL lane_list 4,5,6,7 speed 100000 fec_type RS port_vlan_id 1 admin_state true
# enable port connected to internal Ethernet CPU
add port type NORMAL lane_list 130 speed 10000 fec_type NONE autoneg DEFAULT port_vlan_id 1

If the commands are successful, you should get a member_handle number in the output log. Next, we use the member_handle to add both ports to VLAN 1 (default vlan)

# member handle numbers are given after add port command
add vlan_member member_handle port 4 vlan_handle vlan 1
add vlan_member member_handle port 5 vlan_handle vlan 1

Finally, set IP addresses and routes on both the server and the switch control plane CPU.

On rest-bfsw01:

sudo ip a add 10.10.0.20/24 dev enp4s0f0

On restsrv01 we also need to ensure traffic through the NIC connected to rest-bfsw01. A simple way is to add a /32 routing rule.

sudo ip a add 10.10.0.21/24 dev ens5f1
sudo ip route add 10.10.0.20/32 dev ens5f1

✅ You can now ping the two hosts.

server ↔️ Cisco 100G ↔️ switch.p4 ↔️ rest-bfsw01 cpu

In this scenario, we check for connectivity when passing through the Cisco 100G switch.

Make sure to remove the route added before:

sudo ip route del 10.10.0.20/32 dev ens5f1

Use ip route to double check that the route to the data plane network is via the interface ens5f0.

Then enable the port connected to Cisco 100G:

# enable port 29/0 of rest-bfsw01
add port type NORMAL lane_list 112,113,114,115 speed 100000 fec_type RS port_vlan_id 1 admin_state true
add vlan_member member_handle port 4 vlan_handle vlan 1
add vlan_member member_handle port 5 vlan_handle vlan 1

Ping test should work !

Debug issues

Check port counters with bfshell> ucli.pm show.

Quick steps to debug

item.title: Quick debugging
item.description:
This page provides several examples for quick debugging or troubleshooting your P4 program. The troubleshooting is done using bf-sde, which can be activated from bfsehll:

bfshell> ucli
bf-sde> ?
 dump-trace Display the trace logs
 reset-trace Clear the trace logs
 set-trace-level Set the trace level for a module
 set-log-level Set the log level for a module
 get_trace get_trace <size>
 ver Display versions of all loaded/linked BF SDE components
 show_tech_drivers Display verbose system and module parameters. Usage -d <dev_id> -m <module_name> [-f <to enable file logging>]
 dvm
 lld
 devdiag
 port_mgr
 mc_mgr
 pipe_mgr
 traffic_mgr
 pm
 pkt_mgr
 perf
 switchd

For more detailed testing and troubleshooting guidelines, please refer to Section 9 of Wedge 100B User Guide documentations (NDA required).

Wedge 100B User Guide

Dumping Match-action Tables

You can dump the match and action information of your P4 program using pipe_mgr.

List All Match-action Tables

To list all the tables in use by the P4 program, use the pipe_mgr table dump command, tbl -d <dev>(where <dev> is the switch device ID, usually “0” on a single-ASIC system):

bf-sde.pipe_mgr> tbl -d 0

Match-Action Tables:

----------------------------|----------|-----|--------|-----|----|---|---|---|---|----|----|-----
Name |Handle |Type |Entries |Keysz|Stgs|Adt|Sel|Sta|Met|Sful|Prof|Owner
----------------------------|----------|-----|--------|-----|----|---|---|---|---|----|----|-----
IngressParser.$PORT_METADATA|0x1000001 |exm |288 |0 |0 |NA |NA |NA |NA |NA |0 |P0
Ingress.ipv4_host |0x1000002 |exm |65536 |0 |1 |NA |NA |NA |NA |NA |0 |Exm
Ingress.ipv4_net |0x1000003 |term |65536 |0 |6 |NA |NA |NA |NA |NA |0 |Tcam
Ingress.ipv4_lpm |0x1000004 |term |12288 |0 |1 |NA |NA |NA |NA |NA |0 |Tcam

item.title: Control plane code
item.description:
This page describes how to interact with P4 tables and objects using the interactive bfshell. In this tutorial, we’ll use a simple P4 program called simple_l3 for example, which contains two tables, ipv4_host and ipv4_lpm.

Interactive bfshell

The driver runs a CLI, called bfshell. It is actually a “gateway” to several different interactive shells. A tool with the same name (usually invoked by running the script $SDE/run_bfshell.sh or bfshell) allows you to access bfshell via a telnet-like session from another window. The advantage of this approach is that your session will not be obscured by driver messages.

It is automatically activated after executing p4 -p program with a prompt bfshell>.

Navigating the CLI

At any level of CLI, ? displays the sub-packages and available commands. Type .. to exit a sub-package and return to its parent. exit brings you back to bfshell> root level.

Interacting with P4 Tables using bfshell

Getting bfrt object

At bfshell>, if it’s the fist time to execute bfrt_python , you will get a bfrt_python> prompt, then you have to execute bfrt to get bfrt> prompt. Afterwards, executing bfrt_python at bfshell> will directly return bfrt>.

bfshell> bfrt_python
cwd : <your_pwd>

We've found 1 p4 programs for device 0:
<your program>
Creating tree for dev 0 and program simple_l3

Available symbols:
dump - Command
info - Command
mirror - Node
port - Node
pre - Node
<your program> - Node
tf1 - Node

User-defined Tables

Tables defined in your P4 pipeline is under the hierarchy of bfrt.<your program>.pipe. You may get Egress, EgressParser, Ingress, IngressParser, snapshot depending on your program. For example, we defined two tables in Ingress pipeline in simple_l3, shown as below.

bfrt.simple_l3.pipe.Ingress> info
---------------------------> info()
Tables under this node:
Full Table Name Type Usage Capacity
---------------------- ------------ ------- ----------
pipe.Ingress.ipv4_lpm MATCH_DIRECT 0 12288
pipe.Ingress.ipv4_host MATCH_DIRECT 0 65536

After entering a table, you’ll have the key fields, actions, and a bunch of available commands. Type ? after available actions for help.

bfrt.simple_l3.pipe.Ingress.ipv4_host> ?
BF Runtime CLI Object for pipe.Ingress.ipv4_host table

Key fields:
 hdr.ipv4.dst_addr type=EXACT size=32


Actions, Data fields:
 NoAction (DefaultOnly)
 0 data fields:
 Ingress.drop
 0 data fields:
 Ingress.send
 1 data fields:
 port type=BYTE_STREAM size=9


Available Commands:
add_from_json
add_with_drop
add_with_send
clear
delete
dump
entry_with_drop
entry_with_send
get
get_default
get_handle
get_key
info
mod_with_drop
mod_with_send
reset_default
set_default_with_NoAction
set_default_with_drop
set_default_with_send
symmetric_mode_get
symmetric_mode_set

As you may notice, there are entry_* and add_*. entry_with_<action> just creates a pending entry to be pushed into current table later. add_with_<action> directly adds an entry to current table.

For the helping information of the Available Commands, type ? after the command and execute.

Dumping Tables

To check entries of a specific table, just go to the corresponding level and execute dump.

Adding Entry

Adding an entry can be easily done by calling

add_with_<action>(<match_key_1>=<match_data_1>,...,MATCH_PRIORITY=<prior_value>,<action_key>=<action_data>)

where <action> refers to the available actions of this table, <match_key>, <match_data>, <action_key>, and <action_data> depend on your program. For example, add an entry to ipv4_host as below.

bfrt.simple_l3.pipe.Ingress.ipv4_host> add_with_send(dst_addr='10.0.0.1',port=1)

bfrt.simple_l3.pipe.Ingress.ipv4_host> dump
-------------------------------------> dump()
----- ipv4_host Dump Start -----
Default Entry:
Entry data (action : NoAction):

Entry 0:
Entry key:
 hdr.ipv4.dst_addr : 0x0A000001
Entry data (action : Ingress.send):
 port : 0x01

----- ipv4_host Dump End -----

For inputting the address, bfrt supports both simple string-like address x.x.x.x and ip_address('x.x.x.x') object in Python.

Standard $\rm {P4_{16}}$ supports three types of match_kind, the key-value pairs of which are different.

  • EXACT: <match_key>=<match_value>,...

  • LPM: <match_key>=<match_value>, <match_key>_p_length=<length>

  • TERNARY: <match_key>=<match_value>, <match_key>_mask=<mask>

Besides, Tofino Native Architecture supports two additional match_kind types, i.e., range and selector. Please refer to Tofino Native Architecture Documentation for help.

Open Tofino

Modifying Entry

Similar as adding entry, modifying the action of an existing entry can be done by calling

mod_with_<action>(<match_key_1>=<match_data_1>,...,MATCH_PRIORITY=<prior_value>,<action_key>=<action_data>)

Deleting Entry

delete(<match_key_1>=<match_data_1>,...,MATCH_PRIORITY=<prior_value>)

Fixed Function Tables

You may notice there are other Node options mirror, port, pre, tf1 other than <your program> at bfrt. They are Fixed Functions provided by Tofino ASIC. Official explanation is as below.

To complement the P4 programmable packet processing pipeline, the Tofino ASIC also has ‘Fixed Function’ (FF) blocks. These blocks deal with packet memory buffer management, port configuration, multicast, scheduling, queues, etc. The P4 Studio SDE provides ‘BF Runtime’ API (BF-RT) with data-driven general methods applicable to the different types of Tofino pipeline tables including Exact Match, ALPM, Counters, etc. The same BF-RT API is applicable for the Tofino ‘Fixed Function’ blocks represented as tables.

For details, please refer to BF-Runtime Fixed API Doxygen documentation.

BF-Runtime Fixed API Doxygen Document
  • mirror contains a mirror configuration table called mirror.cfg
  • port contains port configuration tables port, port statistic tables port_stat, etc. for general ports
  • pre contains tables for multicast, copy_to_cpu port
  • tf1 contains tables for packet buffer, queue, scheduling, etc.
Some debugs or diagnostics can be done by dumping entries of these tables. Or you can even configure memory buffer, port, multicast, etc. by modifying the entries. But using BF Runtime API for configuring the Fixed Functions is more suggested, which offers more intuitive operations.

Interacting with P4 Tables using Python scripts

How to run your scripts

Interactive bfshell is very handy for quick debugging or testing. However, if you want to install a batch of rules or configure several ports automatically, interactive bfshell may not be your best choice. Tofino provides a way to interact with switch using Python scripts when running bfshell.

$SDE/run_bfshell.sh [OPTIONS]

Options for running bfshell:
 -f <command_file>
 bfshell command input file.
 -b <python_script>
 bfrt_python script to run.
 -i
 if -b provided, start interactive mode after completion.
 -a <ipv4_addr>
 Connect to this ipv4 address.
 -p <port>
 open connection on this port.
 -d <devices>
 Wait for these devices to be ready (1 or 0-2 or 0,4,6-8)
 --no-status-srv
 Do not query bf_switchd's status server
 --status-port <port number>
 Specify bf_switchd's status server port number; the default is 7777
 -h
 Display this help.

An alternative way is to execute the script from bfshell prompt.

bfrt_python <your_script> <true/false>

The later boolean choice <true/false> is to specify whether to load interactive mode after executing provided script, same as -i option in run_bfshell.sh. One best thing to stay in interactive mode is that from bfrt, you can still access and call functions defined in your script after its execution. In this case, you could just define some helper functions in your script and load it in interactive mode, then call them manually for experiment.

How to write your scripts

The hierarchy and usage of the objects in Python scripts is as same as bfrt.

p4 = bfrt.<your_program>.pipe
pm = bfrt.port
port = bfrt.pre.port
ipv4_lpm = p4.Ingress.ipv4_lpm # a table defined in the P4 program

Adding/modifying/deleting entries are as same as what you did in interactive shell. For example, adding an entry to the table ipv4_lpm in Ingress pipeline is like:

ipv4_lpm.add_with_send(dst_addr=ip_address('192.168.1.0'), dst_addr_p_length=24, port=1)

After executing all operations, the following statement is required at the end of your script.

bfrt.complete_operations()

Enjoy exploring!

item.title: Tofino model (Intel SDE)
item.description:
This page shares some guidelines to run P4 code compiled for a Tofino target on any Linux machine. You need Intel P4 SDE installed.

Intel Tofino Model

The Intel Tofino Model is a software behavioral emulation of the Tofino dataplane chipset. Its goal is specifically to let developers quickly test and debug their code without the need of physically accessing a Tofino ASIC.

The official ICA courses make extensive use of the model!

We warmly recommend (especially new users) to start working with the model first, as it also provides a detailed logging of packet events along the pipeline. This way it is much easier to verify code correctness.

The model is not designed for performance, but for modeling with high fidelity the Tofino chipset. Its peak sustained throughput in quite low (few dozens of packets/sec). It must be used for initial code validation only.

Start the model

In order to exchange traffic between the Tofino model instance running in your local OS and other programs, you must first create a set of veth interfaces and tell the model to connect them to its emulated ports.

Execute iftofinoup to create a default set of veth pairs on the host machine. To check it, use ìp a or ifconfig and see if there are new interfaces veth1, veth2, …, veth251.

> ip a
6: veth1@veth0: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 10240 qdisc noqueue state UP group default qlen 1000

7: veth0@veth1: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 10240 qdisc noqueue state UP group default qlen 1000
 link/ether 1a:c1:2d:55:c2:6a brd ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff
8: veth3@veth2: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 10240 qdisc noqueue state UP group default qlen 1000
 link/ether e6:b8:d2:d1:fd:0d brd ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff
9: veth2@veth3: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 10240 qdisc noqueue state UP group default qlen 1000
 link/ether 86:4d:6b:5d:f9:64 brd ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff

...

71: veth250@veth251: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 10240 qdisc noqueue state UP group default qlen 1000
 link/ether 2a:2a:44:5c:93:66 brd ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff

Next, start the model with the command tfm, which is an alias for:

$SDE/run_tofino_model.sh

If you don’t specify different port-to-veth mapping scheme, by default the model uses the port mapping scheme depicted in .

To specify another mapping scheme, the option -f <port info file>.json when running the model. See the help and the P4 examples coming with the SDE for more details.

Push programs to the model

Once the model has started, you can proceed with the standard way to push P4 programs to your target. This time though, your target will not be a Tofino ASIC, but the Intel Tofino model.

p4 -p program

About choosing between the ASIC and the MODEL modes

how does run_switchd chooses between the ASIC and the MODEL mode?

To put it simply, the run_switchd automatically selects between the MODEL and the ASIC mode, as follows:

  • If a valid Board Support Package (BSP) is present and can be successfully loaded, ASIC mode is selected
  • Otherwise, the MODEL mode is selected

The BSP is a software bundle containing hardware-specific device drivers. When compiling and installing the Intel SDE on rest-bfsw01 and rest-bfsw02 OSes, we provided a BSP tarball for the Edgecore WedgeBF100-32X Tofino switch. The SDE compiling stage produced the /opt/p4-sde/bf-sde-9.13.2/lib/libpltfm_mgr.so system library.

As an example, when we try to run a P4 program from one of the switches CPUs, we get the following output log.

Using the PCIe CPU port

Load the drivers !!! (one of bf_kdrv or bf_kpkt): sudo $SDE_INSTALL/bin/bf_kdrv_mod_load $SDE_INSTALL

Difference between bf_kdrv and bf_kpkt

The difference is that if you use bf_kdrv driver, it allows you to access PCIe CPU port (send/receive packets using packet DMA) at the user-process level, using the specialized bf_pkt APIs, whereas if you use bf_kpkt driver, then the CPU PCIe port is exposed as a regular Linux network interface and you can send/receive packets using any standard Linux methods: you can simply open a raw socket, you can use libpcap, you can use Scapy, Wireshark, etc., etc.) We discuss this in detail in Intel Connectivity Academy course ICA-XFG-101 (formerly that was a part of ICA-1141).

I would say that regardless of the loaded module, when the packet is sent to CPU PCIe port (320 on a 4-pipe Tofino, 192 on a 2-pipe Tofino or port 0 on Tofino2), the packet is automatically sent to the DMA engine. As a result, its contents is placed into the RAM, where the host CPU can access it. The question is: how exactly this RAM will be accessed? In case of bf_kdrv, a process running on the host CPU will see the DMA rings because the driver will map them into the process’ address space. The user process can then use bf_pkt APIs to poll those rings, receive notifications when new packets arrive and ultimately retrieve those packets In case of bf_kpkt, the rings are mapped into the kernel address space and received packets are processed by the standard Linux network interface driver which then makes them accessible via the standard socket interface.

item.title: P4 Insight
item.description:
Introduction

P4 Insight gives you visibility on your P4 program. It is useful to debug and optimize your P4 code. It provides a graphical interface to visualize the P4 program, including the pipeline stages and resource usage.

P4 Insight is a powerful tool, integrated into the Intel® P4 Studio, that gives you unprecedented visibility into your P4 code for fast debugging and powerful optimization.

You can check the detailed user guide of P4 insight at P4 Insight™ User Guide for Release 9.13.1

IMPORTANT: You must compiled with the –g option (./p4c -g) to generate all the required compilation artifacts that p4i works with. You are good to go if you have built your code with the p4-build command.

sudo p4-build program.p4

Requirements

  1. SDE has to be correctly complied and installed (either virtual emulator or physical switch).
  2. Install xvfb as framebuffer
sudo apt install xvfb

Getting Started

Start p4i. You can specify a working directory by adding option -w <dir>.

xvfb-run p4i

Now a P4 Insight instance should be bound to localhost port 3000. You can access it with your browser.

Skip this when using VScode Enable SSH Port forwarding on port if you are accessing via SSH through local terminal:

 ssh -L 3000:localhost:3000 [USER@]SSH_SERVER
  • Open http://localhost:3000/ with your browser.
  • Use the [File...] button in Dashboard (Home page) to browse, select, and load a compilation.
  • Play with P4 Insight! The information displayed on the webpage is very intuitive. For details, please refer to the user guide.

item.title: Tofino access
item.description:
This page describes the policy to access Tofino switches in the cluster. Read access management first.

Reservation dashboard

Users can reserve a time slot on the dashboard, during which they will be granted exclusive ssh access to the switch. See login instructions for more details on how to access the switch.

Access the Tofino reservation dashboard

The interface looks like this:

Rules and Sharing policy

To ensure fair access to all users, the reservation is limited to a maximum of 24h and no more than 3 active reservations can be made at the same time. Users are encouraged to renew their reservation whenever they need by booking a new slot, provided they have less than 3 outstanding reservations at any given time.

We do acknowledge that can be tedious to renew the reservation frequently, however this ensures that all users have a fair chance to access the switches.

We implement two mechanisms to minimize work interruptions:

🎫 Best-effort reservations (default)

By default, each slot you reserve is guaranteed for 24 hours and will become “best-effort” after expiring (i.e., after 24h).

When demoted to best-effort, you still keep a valid access to the switch, until a new user claims the same switch, in which case your reservation will be released and your ssh sessions preempted.

🔴 High-priority reservations

We do acknowledge that in many cases users need urgent and prolonged access to the switches, e.g., for teaching purposes, or paper submission deadlines.

This is not a common use case and should be avoided whenever possible. It will be granted only in special cases.

For these cases we allow users to obtain a non-preemptible reservation. Users must:

  1. create a reservation on the dashboard, as usual;
  2. contact the administrators to obtain a high-priority reservation;
  3. wait for the approval.
Note: Please specify the reason for your request, your username, and the from:to time range you need access to the switch, as inserted in the dashboard.

Once approved, the reservation is flagged as high priority and marked as “urgent” in the dashboard.

item.title: SUP4RNET Website Dev Guide
item.description:
This guide is for developers and mantainers of the SUP4RNET website. You can find the full version of this developer guide on GitHub.

Quick start

The website is written in markdown language (i.e., .md files), then compiled to static html pages using hugo.

Prerequisites

  • Check for existing SSH keys with ls -al ~/.ssh. If you do not have one, please refer to Generating a new SSH key and adding it to the ssh-agent to create a new key.

  • Add your SSH public key to github account. If you already have keys in your github account, jump to step 3. For detail, please see Adding a new SSH key to your GitHub account.

    1. Copy the SSH public key to your clipboard, which is usually saved at ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub or ~/.ssh/rsa.pub.

    2. In the upper-right corner of any page on GitHub, click your profile photo, then click Settings.

    3. In the “Access” section of the sidebar, click SSH and GPG keys.

    4. Click New SSH key or Add SSH key.

    5. Add a Title for the new key as you like. Paste your public key to Key field. Select the type of key, either authentication or signing. Authentication Key is enough for this scenario.

  • Clone this repository on your machine with SSH. This step is for a more convenient pushing to remote repo once you store your SSH public key in Github account.

    git clone git@github.com:sup4rnet/sup4rnet-website.git

    If you have already cloned with HTTPS before, using the following commands to switch the remote URL to ssh.

    # check the remote URL of the local repo
$ git remote -v
origin https://github.com/sup4rnet/sup4rnet-website.git (fetch)
origin https://github.com/sup4rnet/sup4rnet-website.git (push)
# switch to ssh
$ git remote set-url origin git@github.com:sup4rnet/sup4rnet-website.git
# verify
$ git remote -v
origin git@github.com:sup4rnet/sup4rnet-website.git (fetch)
origin git@github.com:sup4rnet/sup4rnet-website.git (push)

  • Install Hugo.

Edit website content

Bring things up

Go into the directory where you cloned the repository and start Hugo.

cd sup4ernet-website
hugo serve

Open your browser and go to localhost:1313.

🎉 Here we go. Hugo just compiled your website. As you will edit one of the markdown files, the website at localhost:1313 will instantly refresh so that you can see your changes quickly.

Since hugo serve has loaded your website in memory, it will be incredibly to refresh your local changes!

Add/modify pages

The markdown files are located in the content folder, and organized in subfolders corresponding to sections of the website.

> tree -L 2 content

content
├── authors
│ ├── admin
│ ├── _index.md
│ └── paolo
├── blog
│ ├── about-multitenancy
│ ├── beta-testing
│ ├── _index.md
│ └── unibo-callegati-joins
├── community
│ ├── ac-2020.jpg
│ └── index.md
├── docs
│ ├── admin
│ ├── _index.md
│ ├── reference.md
│ ├── supernet
│ └── tofino-primer
├── _index.md
├── projects
│ ├── _index.md
│ └── nvidia
└── quickstart
 ├── getstarted
 ├── _index.md
 └── overview

✏️ As an example, edit content/quickstart/_index.md and change the page title. Then browse to localhost:1313/quickstart and your changes are instantaneously there.

You are ready you play with the website.

Deployment

Once you are satisfied with your local changes, the next step is to deploy them in production.

cd deploy
./deploy.sh

The deploy.sh script will attempt to update both the public GitHub pages website and the private website hosted in a local machine within the cluster: restsrv01.polito.it.

Website configuration

We used Hugo Blox docs template. We provide here some useful information, read the doc on the Hugo Blox website for more.

The Hugo Documentation Template empowers with everything you need to build a beautiful documentation website, including a customizable block-based homepage and blog. It’s ultra-fast and easy, letting you focus on your content. It’s also no-code by default, so no JavaScript knowledge is required unlike other templates!

Page layout and metadata

Every .md file in the website has a frontmatter section of this kind:

---
title: Your page title
type: docs
toc: true
---

Here you can specify meta parameters related to the page layout, the page title to be shown in the nav bars, etc. See existing files as an example.

Hugo config files

You can customize pretty much everything in your website via .yaml configuration files in config folder.

  • menu.yaml: specifies which folders correspond to the menu entries on the website
  • hugo.yaml here you can specify some meta parameters for the website. A useful use of this is to cascade your page parameter settings to all pages in a folder. See config/_default/hugo.yaml as an example.
  • params.yaml: here you can specify other things such as website logo, text to be displayed when you share your wesite on social channels (i.e., SEO settings).

Detailed guide

See our Mantainance Guide for more details.

This guide covers how to edit, test, and deploy the Tofino reservation dashboard.

Overview

The dashboard is a Flask web application maintained in a separate repository:

git clone https://github.com/sup4rnet/tofino-reservation-app

Follow the README.md in that repository to set up the local development environment.

Edit the dashboard

Make your changes to the Flask application, then commit and push to the main branch.

Deploy

The deployment infrastructure is located in the deploy folder of the sup4rnet-website repository. The dashboard runs as a Docker container behind a reverse proxy.

Test environment

Before deploying to production, test your changes locally using docker-compose.test.yml:

cd deploy
docker compose -f docker-compose.test.yml up --build -d

This deploys a development environment on port 8001 with:

  • Website at :8001/supernet
  • Dashboard at :8001/dashboard

Production deployment

Once testing is complete:

  1. Identify the commit to deploy - In the tofino-reservation-app repository, find the commit ID:

    git log --oneline

  2. Update the compose file - Edit docker-compose.yml (not docker-compose.test.yml) and set the COMMIT_ID variable to the commit you want to deploy.

Always use docker-compose.yml for production, not docker-compose.test.yml.
  1. Deploy - Run the following command: 
    docker compose up --build -d

The dashboard will be accessible at http://restsrv01.polito.it/dashboard.

item.title: About multi-tenancy on Tofino hardware
item.description:
Given the multi-tenancy nature of the cluster, isolation mechanisms are essential to prevent tenants from interfering with each other and to ensure the ability to run concurrent experiments. Differently from general-purpose compute infrastructure, existing programmable data-plane technologies lack the essential support for multi-tenancy. This is also the case for the Intel Tofino products line.

These switches are equipped with multiple packet processing pipelines that can be programmed individually, thus in principle enabling some form of parallel program execution. However, they do not implement any mechanism for fault, resource and performance isolation across programs of different tenants, which can interfere with each other, either by accident or maliciously. As a result, every time a P4 program is installed, all pipelines undergo a complete reconfiguration, potentially causing disruption to the operations of other tenants’ programs.

Do we have a way to enable concurrent program execution while avoiding interference among tenants?

Virtualizing Hardware Resources for Multi-Tenancy

To enable concurrent program execution while avoiding interference among tenants, there are several approaches that can be considered:

  1. Compile-Time Merging: This approach involves statically combining and compiling the P4 programs of different tenants into a single P4 binary. This merged binary is then installed on the target switch. On this line of work we find P4Visor1. However, the compiling phase and pipeline re-configuration before runtime may require active tedious coordination cycles across tenants.
  1. Hypervisor-Like P4 Programs: Solutions like HyPer42 instead use a hypervisor-like P4 program to dynamically emulate other P4 programs. This approach provides the illusion of multiple data plane programs but incurs significant overheads, limiting its applicability to software and FPGA targets.
  1. Reconfigurable Match-Action (RMT) Hardware Extensions: More recent work, such as Menshen3 propose extensions to the RMT hardware architecture for data-plane multi-tenancy. Menshen adds an indirection layer using small tables to dynamically load different per-tenant configurations for the same RMT resource. While these solutions allow running per-tenant packet processing logic, they are not specifically designed for Tofino hardware.
  1. State-of-the-art transparent virtualization: SwitchVM4 introduces a runtime interpreter that allows the execution of Data Plane Filters (DPFs) in a P4 sandbox environment. SwitchVM does not require pipeline reconfiguration when installing new DPFs, as it involves installing match-action rules that redirect to a fixed set of executable instructions. Similarly to eBPF programs, DPFs are short programs which can be pre-installed on a PISA-like device and whose execution is triggered by arriving packets. In other words, installing new DPFs consists in installing match-action rules that redirect to a fixed set of executable instructions (e.g., ADD, MOV, etc.) implemented as atomic P4 actions, thus not involving any pipeline reconfiguration. Thus, SwitchVM enables time-sharing of the pipeline hardware across multiple tenants. Moreover, it guarantees strict resource isolation between DPFs belonging to different tenants, thanks to virtual registers with load/store instructions to access per-tenant state. It enables time-sharing of the pipeline hardware across multiple tenants and guarantees strict resource isolation between DPFs belonging to different tenants. It effectively achieves transparent virtualization from a hardware standpoint, however tenants must write code using a new instruction set, and not all P4 constructs are reflected into the DPF instruction set. Ultimately, SwitchVM has been implemented on a Tofino target and thus it is an interesting approach to consider for SUPERNET.

These approaches provide ways to virtualize hardware resources and enable concurrent program execution while ensuring isolation among tenants in a multi-tenancy environment. However, not all of them have been tested on Tofino switches, or require some extra effort to the P4 developer.

Initially, we opted for a static resource reservation system which grants exclusive access to the switch to one user at a time, providing isolation but not concurrency on the hardware.

  1. P. Zheng, T. Benson, and C. Hu, “P4visor: lightweight virtualization and composition primitives for building and testing modular programs,” in Proceedings of the 14th International Conference on Emerging Networking EXperiments and Technologies, Association for Computing Machinery, 2018. ↩︎

  2. D. Hancock and J. van der Merwe, “HyPer4: Using P4 to virtualize the programmable dataplane,” in Proceedings of the 12th International on Conference on Emerging Networking EXperiments and Technologies, Association for Computing Machinery, 2016 ↩︎

  3. T. Wang, X. Yang, G. Antichi, A. Sivaraman, and A. Panda, “Isolation mechanisms for High-Speed Packet-Processing pipelines,” in 19th USENIX Symposium on Networked Systems Designand Implementation (NSDI 22). USENIX Association, 2022. ↩︎

  4. S. Khashab, A. Rashelbach, and M. Silberstein, “Multitenant In-Network acceleration with SwitchVM,” in 21st USENIX Symposium on Networked Systems Design and Implementation (NSDI 24). USENIX Association, 2024. ↩︎
